summary: Jesus calls Matthew, also called Levi, from his tax office, eats with tax collectors and sinners at his feast, and answers His critics: He came to call sinners.
key_insight: Luke says Levi “left all,” and the next thing Luke tells is that he opened his house. A tax collector’s friends were tax collectors and sinners, and Levi brought them to the table with Jesus.
story: Jesus went out again by the sea. The whole crowd came to Him, and He taught them. {Mk} As He passed by, He saw a tax collector named Levi, {Lk} the son of Alphaeus, {Mk} sitting at the tax office. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew. {Mt}
Jesus said to him, “Follow Me.” So he left all, rose up, and followed Him. {Lk}
Then Levi gave Jesus a great feast in his own house. {Lk} Many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and His disciples, for there were many, and they followed Him. {Mk}
When the scribes and Pharisees saw Him eating with tax collectors and sinners, they complained to His disciples, “How is it that He eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?” {Mk}

Jesus heard it and answered, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.” {Mt}
differences: Matthew calls him Matthew; Mark and Luke call him Levi, and Mark adds “the son of Alphaeus.”
Luke alone says he “left all” and that Levi gave Jesus “a great feast.” Mark places the meal in Levi’s house; Matthew says only that Jesus sat at the table “in the house.”

The complaint is worded differently: “Why does your Teacher eat” (Matthew), “How is it that He eats and drinks” (Mark), and “Why do You eat and drink” (Luke), where the critics address the disciples themselves.
Only Matthew records Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”
Only Mark sets the call beside the sea, with Jesus teaching the crowd.

fit.question: Matthew’s Gospel says Jesus called “a man named Matthew.” Mark and Luke tell the same call of a tax collector named Levi. Are these two different men?

points.label: Two names, one man
points.text: The details match exactly: the tax office, the words “Follow Me,” the immediate response and the meal that followed. Many Jews of the time had two names, as Simon was also Cephas or Peter, and Saul was also Paul.

points.label: The lists of the Twelve
points.text: Mark and Luke both list Matthew among the Twelve (Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15), and Matthew’s list calls him “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). No tax collector named Levi appears anywhere else among Jesus’ followers.

points.label: How he had both names
points.text: The Gospels do not say whether he carried both names from birth or received the name Matthew, meaning gift of the Lord, after he began to follow Jesus, as Simon received the name Peter.

fit.note: Nothing in the accounts suggests two men, and everything fits one man known by two names.
fit.short: Levi and Matthew are one man with two names, like Simon Peter. Matthew’s Gospel calls him “Matthew the tax collector.”

scene.label: The tax office
scene.text: Capernaum lay near the border between Herod Antipas’s Galilee and the land ruled by his brother Philip, on a road that carried trade. Levi probably collected tolls on goods for Herod’s government rather than taxes paid straight to Rome.

scene.label: Tax collectors
scene.text: The right to collect tolls was often sold to contractors, who profited by taking more than was due (Luke 3:12–13). Jews despised tax collectors as cheats who served foreign-backed rulers, and named them in the same breath as harlots (Matthew 21:31).

scene.label: Eating together
scene.text: Sharing a meal meant accepting someone into fellowship. Pharisees were careful about whom they ate with, to guard ritual purity. To them, Jesus at a table full of tax collectors looked like approval of their way of life.

scene.label: “Sinners”
scene.text: In the Pharisees’ language, sinners could mean notorious wrongdoers, but also ordinary people who did not keep the Law as the Pharisees taught it. Jesus did not deny that His table companions were sick. He came to them as their physician.

witnesses.matthew: Calls him Matthew, and in the list of the Twelve, “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3); only this Gospel keeps that label on him, and early Christian writers name Matthew as its author. He alone records Jesus sending the Pharisees to Hosea 6:6, a verse he quotes again in Matthew 12:7.
witnesses.mark: Names him “Levi the son of Alphaeus” and notes that the tax collectors and sinners at the table were many, “and they followed Him.” In Mark this is the second clash with the religious leaders, and the question has moved from Jesus’ words to His table.
witnesses.luke: Stresses both the cost and the celebration: Levi “left all,” then gave “a great feast.” Luke, who later tells of the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son, and of Zacchaeus (Luke 15; 19:1–10), shows Jesus at table with outsiders again and again.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Physician who goes to the sick. He did not wait for Levi to become respectable; He called him at the tax office and sat at his table with his friends.
seeing.living: If you know you are sick, you are exactly the kind of person Jesus came to call. And if He has called you, open your table as Levi did, so the people you know can meet Him there.
seeing.ponder: Do you see yourself among the “well” who stand outside complaining, or among the sick at Jesus’ table?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus came as a physician for sinners, and He calls them to His table.
preaching.watch_for: Matthew tells this call in nearly the same words as the fishermen’s (Matthew 4:18–19; 9:9): Jesus passes by, sees a man at work and says, “Follow Me.” A despised tax collector receives the same call as the fishermen.
